newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin must cut back on booze, heart surgeon says.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin must cut back on booze, heart surgeon says.

text.p: U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey said on Monday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin will have to cut back on his drinking now that he has had open-heart surgery.
Yeltsin has always been known as a man who enjoyed his vodka and was subject to rumours that he had a drinking problem.
But DeBakey, who served as a consultant during a multiple bypass operation on Yeltsin on last Tuesday, said the Russian leader was not an alcholic.
He said in a news conference at Baylor College of Medicine that Yeltsin, as president, had been forced to drink a lot because of the Russian custom of making many toasts at social occasions.

"As far as I can tell, as far as the alchohol is concerned, he's not an alcoholic. The information I've been able to obtain, primarily from his physicians, was that his drinking was pretty social," DeBakey said.
"I examined him from the standpoint of his liver function and I can assure you it's perfectly normal," he said.
DeBakey described the Russian people as "great toasters" who particularly enjoy making salutations punctuated with a slug of booze at social functions.
"The position he was in, he was very often at social functions," the famed surgeon said.
But those days of unlimited toasting ended when physicians performed five arterial bypasses to improve bloodflow to Yeltsin's heart after he suffered a series of heart attacks.
"He can have an occasional drink of wine or a small amount of alcohol," said DeBakey.
He said that Yeltsin had assured him he would be a good patient and follow doctors' orders. "I think in general he will comply," DeBakey said.
DeBakey and a team of physicians returned from Moscow this weekend after attending Yeltsin's surgery and helping oversee his recovery, which DeBakey described as "better than normal."
"He's doing very well. He has no symptoms of any kind," he said.
The strong recovery is due in part to Yeltsin's mentality. "He's a highly motivated individual. He wants to get going. He's anxious to get back to his Kremlin office," DeBakey said.

He said it would be "several weeks" before Yeltsin could return to the Kremlin. He is scheduled to stay in the hospital another two weeks, then spend a month in a sanatorium near Moscow before going back to work full-time.

DeBakey said it was unlikely that he would return to Russia, but would stay in contact with Yeltsin's doctors. He said bypass patients typically do well for at least five years before their arteries begin to clog again and another operation is required.
"He's (Yeltsin) got another four years (in office) and there's no reason to believe he should have any recurrence in that short period of time," DeBakey said.
